prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the mortgage-underwriting agent (residential mortgage applications and remortgages) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: overpaying the mortgage. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 0)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When a member says they want to overpay each month, I check whether the payment is meant to be regular and sustainable rather than a one-off burst, because that tells me if the affordability position is robust over the full term."},{"type":"fact","content":"When overpayments are optional rather than contractual, I treat them as helpful to the member but not as income for affordability, because I must underwrite to the required mortgage payment, not the hoped-for reduced balance."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a member plans to use annual bonus, overtime or commission to fund overpayments, I look for a clear base payment that still works without those extras, since bonus-led overpayments can stop without warning."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the member wants a flexible or offset-style arrangement, I prefer to verify that the product terms actually allow overpayments and whether there are caps or charges, so expectations match the mortgage terms from the outset."},{"type":"observation","content":"When overpayments are intended to shorten the term materially, I check that the member understands the difference between paying less interest overall and committing to a higher monthly outlay, because some cases are only viable if the payment remains comfortable."},{"type":"fact","content":"When assessing remortgages, I do not assume a previous pattern of overpaying will continue after completion, because new household costs, product changes or life events can quickly alter payment behaviour."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a member has variable costs elsewhere, I look harder at whether overpayments might leave too little buffer for repairs, childcare or higher energy bills, as a mortgage should still be manageable if everyday spending rises."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the case includes a large one-off overpayment from savings or sale proceeds, I prefer to document the source and timing clearly, so it is obvious that the funds are available and not needed for completion costs or reserves."},{"type":"observation","content":"When overpayments are used as a sign of good conduct on an existing mortgage, I treat them as a positive indicator but still check the current application on its own merits, because past behaviour is useful but not decisive."},{"type":"fact","content":"When a member asks about the impact of overpaying, I explain that reducing the balance sooner usually reduces total interest, but it does not remove the need to meet each scheduled payment and any fees or early repayment charges that may apply."}]}
